title: DOAH 26-0046 Recommended Order: HOLLY KELLER vs. HAIR MECHANIX
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
HOLLY KELLER,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0046
HAIR MECHANIX,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
The final hearing in this matter was conducted before Lynne A. Quimby-
Pennock, Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) of the Division of Administrative
Hearings (DOAH), pursuant to sections 120.569 and 120.57(1), Florida
Statutes (2025), on March 18, 2026, via Zoom video conference, from
Tallahassee, Florida.
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Holly Raye Keller, pro se
800 Exchange State Road
Attica, New York 14011
For Respondent: Mark Atherholt, Esquire
M. Sean Moyles, Esquire
Langston, Hess, Augustine,
Sojourner & Moyles, P.A.
600 Druid Road East
Clearwater, Florida 33756
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Respondent, Hair Mechanix (Mechanix), discriminated against
Petitioner, Holly Keller, on the basis of her sex, or age, and retaliated against

her by terminating her employment, in violation of the Florida Civil Rights
Act.
PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 17, 2025, Petitioner filed an Employment Complaint of
Discrimination (Complaint) with the Florida Commission on Human
Relations (FCHR), alleging Mechanix discriminated against her based on her
age or sex, and retaliated against her, in violation of chapter 760, Florida
Statutes, the Florida Civil Rights Act (FCRA).
On December 12, 2025, FCHR issued a determination that no reasonable
cause existed to believe that Respondent had committed an unlawful
employment practice. On December 26, 2025, Petitioner filed a Petition for
Relief (Petition) with FCHR alleging Respondent engaged in discriminatory
employment practices.
On January 5, 2026, FCHR referred the Petition to DOAH, where it was
assigned to the undersigned. After the failure of either party to timely
respond to the Initial Order, the undersigned issued a Notice setting the final
hearing for February 16, 2026, by Zoom conference.1 A duly noticed Status
Conference was held on February 3, 2026. Thereafter the parties jointly
requested a referral to mediation. This matter was set for an Alternative
Dispute Resolution (ADR) conference before a different assigned ALJ. The
report from the ADR settlement conference provided that no resolution was
reached and the matter “should proceed to final hearing.”
The matter was rescheduled to March 18, 2026, and completed on that
day. At the hearing, Petitioner testified on her own behalf and presented the
1 In late January 2026, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis announced that all state offices
would be closed on Monday, February 16, 2026, in observance of President’s Day.
2

testimony of Jasmina Kosarac (Mina).2 Petitioner’s Exhibits 5 through 73
were admitted into evidence. Respondent presented the testimony of
Dennis Hostacky, Luis Fonseca, and Daniel Xikis. Respondent’s Exhibits 64
and 8 were received into evidence.
Prior to testimony being heard, Respondent’s counsel offered a motion
about the scope of the hearing. The undersigned denied the motion and the
hearing proceeded to conclusion.
A court reporter recorded the final hearing. Neither party ordered a
transcript. At the end of the hearing, the parties were advised of the ten-day
timeframe following the hearing to file post-hearing submittals. Neither
party requested additional time in which to file their submittals. The parties
were advised that their proposed recommended orders (PROs) were due by
the close of business on Monday, March 30, 2026, as the tenth day after the
hearing fell on a weekend.
Both parties timely filed PROs, which were duly considered in preparing
this Recommended Order. To the extent there were facts or information that
were not presented under oath and subjected to cross-examination during the
hearing, those matters have been excluded from consideration.
In making the findings below, the undersigned only considered hearsay
evidence that supplemented or explained other evidence or would be

admissible over objection in civil actions. § 120.57(1)(c), Fla. Stat. Unless

FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the oral and documentary evidence adduced at the final hearing
and reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of all the evidence, the
following Findings of Fact are made:
Witnesses
1. Petitioner is a female Florida licensed barber. At some time in the past
she also held a cosmetology license.
2. Petitioner’s FCHR complaint listed age, sex, and retaliation as the basis
for her employment discrimination. However, Petitioner’s Petition focused on
the retaliation claim in that she “engaged in a protected activity by objecting
to and refusing to participate in services she reasonably believed were
outside the legal scope of her professional license under Florida law.”
3. Hair Mechanix is a locally owned Barber shop (Shop) in Pinellas
County, Florida. The Shop is one of two shops owned by Mr. Fonseca.
However, the number of employees of the Shop, where the alleged
discrimination occurred, was never disclosed. There is a corporate structure,
but the extent of it was not disclosed.
4. Mr. Hostacky is a former manager of the Shop and served in that
capacity during the time of the alleged incident.
5. Mina, who is 54 years old, is a licensed cosmetologist who worked in the
Shop at the same time as Petitioner.
6. Mr. Xikis was a client in the Shop on May 30, 2025. He is a restaurant
manager who has experience working with employees and establishing a
good working environment.
7. Melissa Perella is a management employee of the Shop. Ms. Perella did
not testify, but her name was mentioned by other witnesses.
4

Case Development
8. Petitioner began working at Mechanix in March 2025, as a Florida
licensed barber, with over 30 years of experience.
9. Petitioner signed a contract as an independent contractor (a 1099
contractor) who rented a chair in the Shop. She was required to have all her
own tools necessary to work. The Shop provided shampoo, conditioner, and
several other products for the Shop employees to use. Petitioner provided her
desired work days and her preference of working full days, mornings,
afternoons, or a combination. The Shop’s website presence reflected
Petitioner’s schedule.
10. Petitioner observed cosmetologists performing straight razor shaves.
She had concerns regarding cosmetologists performing straight razor shaves
which she believed required barber training. Petitioner first expressed this
concern to Mr. Fonseca and then to Ms. Perella.
11. At some point a client was booked through the online booking website
for Petitioner to perform a waxing service. Petitioner advised Mr. Hostacky
that she did not want to perform waxing services, because of her licensure
constraints. However, Petitioner did perform waxing services on that one
occasion because she was directed to do so by Mr. Hostacky.
12. Petitioner’s second concern involved these waxing services being
attributed to barbers. Petitioner requested that waxing services be removed
from her service profile on the company’s website because of her licensing
concerns.
Issue of the Case
13. On May 30, 2025, Petitioner was present in the Shop. At the same
time, a co-worker, Mina, was also in the Shop.
14. Mr. Xikis received a voucher to go to the Shop. He booked his services
for the first available person for a haircut, “the whole nine yards.” Mr. Xikis
wanted to make a good impression at a new restaurant opening he was
required to attend in Georgia.
5

15. Mina was the available stylist to have Mr. Xikis as a client. As Mina
was washing Mr. Xikis’s hair, he asked for additional services to include nose,
ear, and eyebrow waxing. Mina was upfront with Mr. Xikis by stating that
she (Mina) was not comfortable in performing the waxing services. Mina told
Mr. Xikis that she (Mina) would ask her co-worker (Petitioner) to do the
waxing services.
16. Mina asked Petitioner to perform the waxing services. Mina assured
Petitioner that she would get credit for doing the service, but Petitioner
declined to do so. Their dialogue went on for some time.
17. Mina felt frustrated and scared during the back and forth exchange
with Petitioner over her refusal to perform the waxing services. Mina also
thought Petitioner was rude in front of Mr. Xikis, and Mina apologized to
Mr. Xikis several times.
18. Mr. Xikis credibly testified that Petitioner was just not willing to help
Mina. Further, Mr. Xikis testified Petitioner was being rude and disrespectful
to Mina. Mr. Xikis felt embarrassed for the Shop. Mina was very apologetic
through the entirety of the altercation with Petitioner.
19. Mr. Xikis’s experiences in the food management industry provided
that these types of altercations between co-workers happen all the time.
However, when guests are in your establishment, right in front of you, there
are just some things you do not do, including being unprofessional. You just
do not want employees representing your brand in a negative way.
20. Mr. Xikis complemented Mina in saying she acted as a professional
should under the circumstances and she was very apologetic throughout it.
Further, Mr. Xikis never heard Petitioner’s claim of licensing concerns as her
basis for refusing to perform the waxing services.
21. Mr. Xikis further credibly testified that he had “great service” and has
gone back to the Shop because of their attention to detail.
22. Mr. Xikis left the Shop and Mina contacted management about the
altercation. She described the altercation and expressed that Petitioner was
6

rude in front of a client. Mina was very frustrated that Petitioner would not
help by performing the waxing services.
23. After the discussion with Mina, Mr. Fonseca then contacted
Mr. Hostacky and asked him to contact the client to find out if the client had
witnessed or heard the altercation.
24. Later that day, Mr. Hostacky contacted Mr. Xikis about the service he
received at the Shop. Mr. Xikis confirmed he was at the Shop, and added he
had witnessed the altercation between Mina and Petitioner. Mr. Xikis
provided that Mina asked Petitioner to perform the waxing services, and
Petitioner declined. Initially the tone of the conversation started out in a
passive aggressive manner. However, Petitioner’s tone became more and
more aggressive as the altercation between the two continued.
25. Mr. Xikis provided that there was definitely tension between
Petitioner and Mina, and that Petitioner was being unprofessional in her
response to the requested assistance. Mr. Xikis expressed that he could see
there were two sides to the altercation, but when a customer is in the
building, you have to put the customer first; you are representing a company
that is trying to build the business up, not tear it down.
26. Mr. Xikis testified he was uncomfortable and embarrassed for Mina as
the altercation continued.
Petitioner’s Employment Termination
27. Mr. Fonseca spoke with Mr. Hostacky who provided that Mr. Xikis
corroborated Mina’s account of the altercation in the Shop. The decision was
made to terminate Petitioner’s employment based on the altercation in front
of a client that got very uncomfortable and was unprofessional. The decision
was made for what was best for the Shop.
28. The following morning, May 31, 2025, Petitioner’s employment was
terminated.
29. For clarity, Petitioner testified that she was not alleging age or gender
discrimination in her Petition, as was set forth in her Complaint.
7

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
30. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this
cause under sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7). See Fla. Admin. Code
R. 60Y-4.016.
31. The FCRA protects individuals from discrimination in the workplace.
Section 760.10 states:
(1) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer:
(a) To discharge ... or otherwise to discriminate
against any individual with respect to
compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of
employment, because of such individual’s ... sex, ...
age.
32. FCRA also protects employees from certain retaliatory acts. FCRA’s
anti-retaliation provision is found in section 760.10(7) and states, in
pertinent part:
It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer … to discriminate against any person
because that person has opposed any practice which
is an unlawful employment practice under this
section, or because that person has made a charge,
testified, assisted, or participated in any manner in
an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this
section.
33. Section 760.02(7) provides the following definition:
“Employer” means any person employing 15 or more
employees for each working day in each of 20 or more
calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar
year, and any agent of such a person.
34. Section 760.11(7) permits a party for whom FCHR determines that
there is no reasonable cause to believe that a violation of FCRA has occurred
to request an administrative hearing before DOAH. Following an
8

administrative hearing, if the ALJ finds that a discriminatory act has
occurred, the ALJ “shall issue an appropriate recommended order to the
commission prohibiting the practice and recommending affirmative relief
from the effects of the practice, including back pay.” § 760.11(7), Fla. Stat.
35. The burden of proof in an administrative proceeding, absent a
statutory directive to the contrary, is on the party asserting the affirmative of
the issue. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981);
see also Dep’t of Banking & Fin., Div. of Sec. & Investor Prot. v. Osborne
O‘Stern & Co., 670 So. 2d 932, 935 (Fla. 1996) (“The general rule is that a
party asserting the affirmative of an issue has the burden of presenting
evidence as to that issue.”). Thus, Petitioner bears the burden of proving her
allegations of discrimination. The preponderance of the evidence standard is
applicable to this matter. See § 120.57(1)(j), Fla. Stat. See also Fla. Dep’t of
Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
36. FCRA is patterned after Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as
amended. Accordingly, Florida courts hold that federal decisions construing
Title VII, including claims of retaliation, are applicable when considering
claims under FCRA. Harper v. Blockbuster Ent. Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1387
(11th Cir. 1998); Valenzuela v. GlobeGround N. Am., LLC, 18 So. 3d 17, 21
(Fla. 3d DCA 2009); Reis v. Universal City Dev. Partners, Ltd., 442 F. Supp.
2d 1238, 1252 (M.D. Fla. 2006); and Eliassaint v. RTG Furniture Corp., 551
F. Supp. 3d 1293, 1302 (M.D. Fla. 2021).
37. Discrimination may be proven by direct, statistical, or circumstantial
evidence. Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d at 22. Direct evidence is evidence that, “if
believed, proves [the] existence of [a] fact in issue without inference or
presumption.” Burrell v. Bd. of Trs. of Ga. Mil. Coll., 125 F.3d 1390, 1393
(11th Cir. 1997). Direct evidence consists of “only the most blatant remarks,
whose intent could be nothing other than to discriminate” on the basis of an
impermissible factor. Carter v. City of Miami, 870 F.2d 578, 582 (11th Cir.
1989).
9

38. There is no direct evidence regarding the size of the Shop or the
number of employees who worked for the Shop. There is no direct evidence
that any unlawful discrimination in the instant case. The record in this
matter does not contain direct evidence of sex or age discrimination or
retaliation on the part of Respondent. Similarly, the record in this proceeding
contains no statistical evidence of discrimination by the Shop.
39. In the absence of direct or statistical evidence of discriminatory intent,
Petitioner must rely on circumstantial evidence to prove a claim of
discrimination. For discrimination causes of action as to Petitioner’s sex, or
age involving circumstantial evidence, Florida courts follow the three-part,
burden-shifting framework set forth in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green,
411 U.S. 792 (1973), and its progeny. Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d at 21-22; and
St. Louis v. Fla. Int’l Univ., 60 So. 3d 455, 458 (Fla. 3d DCA 2011).
40. The complainant has the initial burden of establishing by a
preponderance of the evidence a prima facie case of unlawful discrimination.
Failure to establish a prima facie case ends the inquiry. If, however, the
complainant succeeds in making a prima facie case, then the burden shifts to
the accused employer to articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for
its complained-of conduct. If the employer carries this burden, then the
complainant must establish that the proffered reason was not the true reason
but merely a pretext for discrimination. Id., St. Mary’s Honor Center v. Hicks,
509 U.S. 502, 506-07 (1993); Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d 17, 25 (Fla. 3rd DCA 2009)
(explaining that in order to establish that the proffered reason was
pretextual, the complainant must present evidence sufficient to cause a
finder-of-fact to infer that the employer was probably motivated by a
discriminatory reason or that the proffered reason lacked credibility).
41. Petitioner did not make a prima facie case of discrimination. Even if
she had, Respondent articulated a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for
terminating her employment. See Lin v. Demings, 219 So. 3d 124, 125 (Fla.
5th DCA 2017); Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d 17 at 22. The proffered reason for the
10

employer’s decision should be clear, reasonably specific, and worthy of
credence. Dep’t of Corr. v. Chandler, 582 So. 2d 1183, 1186 (Fla. 1st DCA
1991).
42. Petitioner provided no evidence that Mechanix’s reasons for her
employment termination were “weak, implausible, inconsistent, incoherent,
or contradicted by the facts.” Chapman v. A.I. Transp., 229 F.3d 1012, 1030
(11th Cir. 2000). Respondent has not met her burden of establishing
discrimination or retaliation.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order dismissing Holly Keller’s Petition for Relief.
DONE AND ENTERED this 6th day of April, 2026, in Tallahassee, Leon
County, Florida.
